title: 'I've not killed the Loch Ness Monster … I've written a manual on how to see it!' - new book by Adrian Shine illuminates mysteries of world-famous waterbody
excerpt: He is a “sympathetic sceptic” when it comes to talk of a monster lurking within Loch Ness. So why does Adrian Shine say the great beast ‘exists’?
content:
He is a renowned authority on Loch Ness and a “sympathetic sceptic” when it comes to talk of a monster lurking within it.

So why, then, does veteran naturalist and respected Nessie investigator Adrian Shine suggest most sightings of the world-famous beast are genuine?

Published on October 20 by Whittles Publishing for Porto Press, ‘A Naturalist’s View of the Loch Ness Enigma’ will offer his definitive conclusions on the loch’s mysteries, drawn from a lifetime of scientific research.

“I say the Loch Ness monster does exist. I've written a manual on how it can be seen,” he tells us.

Mr Shine has long since satisfied himself that the ‘Jurassic Park’ type of long-necked beast and the classic humped version - anything monstrously large - could never inhabit those nutrient poor waters.

He first moved to the lochside in 1973 and by 1975 had satisfied himself there was no monster, yet he stayed another 50-plus years.

As the book – successor to ‘A Natural History of Sea Serpents’ – conveys, Mr Shine is convinced Nessie, the phenomenon, is real.

The caveat is that it exists only in our minds, an explainable product of human perception, psychology, as well as the influence of the unique geography, geology and physics of the loch.

The book not only charts the history of Loch Ness investigations, including the hoaxes and fakery, but delves deep into his theories as to why so many genuine, earnest individuals report similar sightings.

By committing his findings and famous scepticism to print, Mr Shine admits he risks courting controversy. The loch’s famously elusive inhabitant has generated vast income and employment within the local tourism industry.

But he insists the mystery and mythology surrounding the loch will easily survive publication of his own thoughts and theories.

“I've been doing this for quite a long time and I have been under pressure to produce, if you like, my final thoughts,” he explained.

“That's what I've done. Loch Ness has been a vehicle, in personal terms, for pursuing my wider interests.

“But I do not deny having in my boyhood, even my adolescence, a young man’s interest in lake monsters and sea serpents.

“I saw a sea serpent, clear as day, in 1957 when I was nearly eight years old on the east coast of England, a place called Mundesley (Norfolk) where I'd been taken by my parents.

“I saw this classic line of humps by the horizon. That, I think, struck the spark.

“But the next day, a local man told me it was actually birds flying in line. That bred the sort of sympathetic scepticism for which I'm very happy to be known.

“Sympathetic scepticism is not a matter of being patronising, it is about being interested in a subject which interests a lot of people.

“How is it that over a thousand honest and sober people are reporting things they interpret as large animals, large unusual ones, in Loch Ness when nobody can find one?

“That's the paradox. The heart of the subject is what people see or, rather, what they perceive to see. That is what I have explained in this book.”

Mr Shine founded the Loch Ness Project, a research group focused on the scientific exploration and investigation of the loch and its famous monster.

In 1987, he led Operation Deepscan, which saw a flotilla of 24 boats carrying a full-length sonar sweep of its waters, generating international coverage.

Then, in 1994, he devised the Rosetta Project, which drilled six 19ft deep “time capsule” sediment cores from the bed of Loch Ness.

He was first attracted to the study of Loch Ness through reading the books of Tim Dinsdale, but ventured first to Loch Morar on the west coast because of the activities of a group called the Loch Morar Survey, led by Elizabeth Montgomery Campbell between 1970 and 1972.

“I noticed in 1969 there was this story of a boat on Morar being rammed by a water beast, Morag, as they came to call her, for which there is as good a pedigree in some respects as for Loch Ness, not in quantity, but certainly in quality,” he said.

“And it struck me, well, Morar is only half the length of Loch Ness, so it must be twice as easy! Well, it didn't work out that way.

“I went and rode a rowing boat around Loch Morar, camping at night in a cheap tent. I had a narrow beam lamp, a very powerful one, and a sea anchor.

“I would row off upwind from my little tent at night, because I knew creatures great and small come up to the surface at night, drop the sea anchor, you know, which retarded my drift, and drift back.

“(It was) a sort of live baiting experiment, if you like!

“It was strenuous by day and chilly by night, but I did have an encounter with a monstrous hump, but it turned out to be a rock about four inches high - a perceptual illusion of the sort I now write about.”

A portion of the book re-examines the famous photographs, but only those Mr Shine was personally involved with as a researcher.

“Loch Ness has taken up the greatest portion of my life, I can't deny it. And I still have that sympathetic scepticism,” he said.

“But I do believe that I have found the answer to the dominant forms of Loch Ness Monster that have been seen.

“One is the multi-humped, classic sea serpent form, but the other one is the alleged Jurassic survivor, the plesiosaur, with its long neck, stumpy body and four flippers.

“That’s what people would love, we'd all love that.

“Through the book I look at how it is that people see those long necks on Loch Ness, those multi-humps, and the upturned boat form, which is the hardest in some ways to explain.

“I think I've done that.

“And there is the form which might look a bit less like an animal, but is deduced to be an animal because it swims upwind.

“That one is due to the special physics of Loch Ness, resulting in it being long and straight, and in line with our prevailing wind.

“It moves the warm water up to one end, pins it there, and then when the wind drops it all flows back and it will bring floating objects against any remaining wind.

“That's the synopsis. There are special things about Loch Ness. Some are geographical and some of them are human induced, with the canal bringing vessels to the loch.

“My plea to everyone is to remember this book is not going to harm the economy, although I realise that not everybody's going to like it because it does provide explanations.

“Even the exhibitions embrace the whole spectrum of opinion.

“People who want to believe in the Loch Ness monster are going to believe in it as long as they want to.

“Remember, the original Loch Ness investigation was called the Loch Ness Phenomenon Investigation Bureau.

“They were looking to find the cause of what people were perceiving. It was very scientific, a phenomenon. And that's the point.

“I say the Loch Ness Monster does exist. I've just written a manual on how it can be seen, the various forms and manifestations of it. It doesn't denigrate the eyewitnesses, it vindicates them because those forms of illusion truly happen.

“The people are describing, very accurately often, what they are seeing or what they are perceiving.

“I have not killed the Loch Ness Monster! I've written a manual. That's it.”
